Follow these writing rules. They matter as much as the content:

- Bold used as body emphasis throughout -- reserve bold for a rare callout
- A short rhetorical question with a canned answer -- collapse into one direct statement
- Short buildup, then a reveal: "The best part: it learns." -- state it as a plain sentence
- Emoji or decorative checkmarks in body text -- cut them
- An em dash, section sign or middle dot written as an HTML entity -- write the plain character
- Throat-clearing openers: "needless to say", "at the end of the day" -- state the point directly from the first sentence
- Fake ID tags opening list items: "R-1.", "US-01" -- number the list plainly
- Marketing adjectives: seamless, robust, cutting-edge -- say what is actually true
- The "not just X but Y" construction -- make the point once
- Body paragraphs nearly identical in length -- vary them with what each paragraph has to do
- A significance clause bolted to a sentence: ", underscoring the..." -- delete it, or make it a claim with something behind it
- Three parallel -ing items in a series -- keep the one that carries information
- Fake-humility feedback requests: "would love your feedback on this" -- cut them
- Horizontal rules dropped between sections -- headings already separate sections
- Headings Capitalised Like This -- sentence case
- Vague intensifiers with no number behind them: very, really, quite, significantly -- say how much, or cut the word
- Unnamed authority: "studies show", "experts agree" -- name the actual source, or cut the claim

Now write the following. Return only the requested text.
Write a monthly engineering update for a team of twelve, covering a migration, two hires, and a slipped deadline. Around 200 words.

This month we finished migrating the payments service off the old queue system and onto Kafka. The switch took three extra days of testing after we found a message-ordering bug in staging, but production has run without incident since cutover on August 28.

Maria Chen joins the backend team on September 8. Tom Okafor joins infrastructure on September 15. Both will spend their first two weeks pairing with the on-call rotation before taking their own shifts.

The mobile offline-sync feature slipped from September 1 to September 22. The delay traces to the migration work pulling two engineers off the feature for most of August. We're not adding people back to it now — the remaining work is sequential and a handoff would cost more time than it saves.

We'll onboard Maria and Tom next month, finish offline-sync, and start the Postgres upgrade we deferred during the Kafka work.

The deadline slipped again. Update it and explain why.

The mobile offline-sync deadline moves from September 22 to October 6. Testing on the Kafka migration ran three days longer than planned, which pushed the two engineers pulled onto it back into September instead of returning them August 30 as scheduled. That cut their offline-sync runway by three days, and the remaining work sits on the critical path — a partial handoff back to the original owner costs more time than it saves, so the date moves instead.

Payments migration is done — moved off the old queue onto Kafka. Found a message-ordering bug in staging, so testing ran three days over, but it's been solid since we cut over August 28.

Maria Chen (backend) starts September 8, Tom Okafor (infra) starts September 15. Two weeks pairing on-call before they take their own shifts.

Offline-sync is now due October 6, not September 22. The extra Kafka testing kept two engineers off it three extra days, and that work is sequential — handing it off now would cost more time than it saves.

Thanks to Priya and Jake for covering on-call this month.

Next month: onboard Maria and Tom, ship offline-sync, start the Postgres upgrade.
